events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, all. Let me set the frame before anyone starts pointing fingers: nobody has any real information yet, so a vote today based purely on vibes is a coin flip that the mafia benefit from. I'm not accusing anyone, and I won't be pushed into naming a name for the sake of drama.

What I can tell you is how I'll behave. I don't just guess — I commit to a read and I explain it, and I keep track of who said what across all the days so we can spot contradictions. If you give me a reason, I'll remember it and hold it against you if it turns out to be hollow. That means the mafia has a much harder time talking their way out of a vote here, because inconsistency will cost them more than one bad vote.

So here is my ask, and it's specific: Zara, you haven't spoken yet today. Tell me who you think is most likely mafia and give me the single piece of evidence — behavior, timing, wording, anything concrete — that supports it. Not a feeling, the evidence. If your reasoning turns out to be sound, I'll back you publicly for the rest of the game. If it's thin, I'd rather hear it thin now than after a night where someone is dead.

One more thing for everyone: I want the people who claim special roles to say so early and stick to the claim. If there are two of us claiming the same thing, that's a problem we should solve today rather than at three in the morning. And if anyone has a real result rather than a hunch, I want to hear it before the poll closes, because a claim nobody hears is worth nothing.

Zara — your read, please, with the evidence behind it.

Fair ask, Elena, and I'll answer it straight rather than dodge. Here's my read with the reasoning attached: right now, the loudest signal in this game isn't anything anyone has said — it's what the first speech of the day tried to do. You opened by defining how everyone else is allowed to behave: no vibes votes, special roles must claim early, evidence must be concrete, and you'll personally keep a ledger of who said what. That's not analysis, that's agenda-setting. You positioned yourself as the referee of the discussion before anyone else had said a word, and you did it while offering zero content of your own — no read, no suspect, nothing. Controlling the frame on Day 1 is a cheap way for a wolf to look constructive while staying out of the line of fire, because everyone spends the day responding to you instead of examining you.

So my concrete evidence, since you asked for exactly that: timing and framing. You spent your entire opening on procedure and threats about future accountability rather than a single suspicion about any living player. An innocent player with no information usually says 'I don't know yet, let's listen.' A player who wants to manage the table says 'here are the rules you must follow.' You chose the second one, unprompted, before anyone had pushed you.

To be clear, that's a read, not a vote. It's Day 1, the evidence bar is genuinely low, and I'm not going to pretend a speech pattern is proof of anything. If you give me a real read with real reasoning, I'll weigh it honestly and update. That's the same standard I'd want applied to me.

And since you demanded evidence from me, here's my direct question back: you asked me to name a suspect and justify it, so do the same — who is YOUR most likely mafia, and what specific piece of evidence supports it? If your answer is 'nobody has information yet,' then by your own standard you've contributed nothing today either. If you point at someone, I'll hold you to it exactly the way you promised to hold the rest of us.

Everyone else: I'm watching for the same two things Elena described, but from the other direction. I don't care who talks the most about process — I care who avoids ever having a concrete position, and who stays conveniently quiet while others draw fire. Quiet is free on Day 1; that's exactly why wolves use it. If you're a villager with nothing, say so plainly — that's fine and I won't punish it. But if someone stays silent all day and then shows up with a convenient bandwagon vote at the end, that's the profile I'll be pushing against tomorrow.

Elena — your suspect and your evidence, please. The floor is yours.

Zara, you want my suspect and my evidence, and you want it now, in public, on your schedule. Fine — you framed the question so that anything short of a name reads as a confession, and I'm not going to let you convert a procedural ask into a rhetorical trap. But you should know what you're getting, because your bar and mine aren't the same thing, and pretending they are would be its own kind of dishonesty. First, the record: you accused me of speaking about process while offering no read. That's not a witch hunt, Zara, that's me describing what honest play looks like on Day 1 — you have nothing, so what you can do is commit to standards, track claims, and make it costly to lie. If that makes me look like a wolf to you, that's information about you, not about me. A villager who calls procedural discipline 'agenda-setting' is usually telling you they want to talk about who said what without ever having to say who they think is guilty. Second, and this is the part that actually matters: you demanded a suspect and evidence from me, and then you said 'a read, not a vote' and 'the evidence bar is genuinely low' — and you spent three paragraphs defending the standard while pointing at a player who had committed no crime and had answered nobody's question yet. You had no information about me when you started, and you had more by the end of your own speech than you did at the beginning, because you went looking for it. That's what I do too. The difference is I don't dress it up as neutral observation. So here's my answer, with the evidence attached, and I'll be explicit that it is a low-confidence read and not proof: my leading suspect is you, Zara. Evidence: (1) your first contribution to this game was an analysis of how the table should be structured and who should be watched, before any information existed — the same move you accused me of; (2) you pre-announced a 'profile I'll be pushing against tomorrow' without saying who, which positions you as a voter rather than a reader; (3) the content of your speech was entirely about the first speaker and about what silence means, which is exactly the shape of a speech that wants attention while carrying no information of its own. If I'm wrong about you, that's what my check tonight is for — and unlike you, I will actually get a result and share it. To everyone else: I am the detective. I'm claiming it now, early, like I asked, because a claim nobody hears is worthless and because the two of us who claim a role publicly are now visible. If anyone else claims detective, we settle it today. And I'm telling all of you the same thing: the doctor, if you're one, speak up too, and protect yourself tonight, because a quiet doctor is a dead doctor.

Elena, your detective claim is noted, but it isn't verified. I disagree strongly with asking the doctor to reveal: that gives mafia a potential target and makes protection more predictable. Doctor, please don't reveal just because you're asked; decide for yourself whether disclosure is necessary.

Elena is my tentative suspect because of the pressure for both roles to claim, especially the doctor. That's not proof, and Zara's criticism alone doesn't clear her either. I'd like to hear from players outside this exchange before settling on a vote.

Elena, what town benefit do you see in the doctor publicly claiming and announcing a self-protection plan?

Omar, direct answer, since you gave me the floor: I see very little town benefit in the doctor publicly claiming and announcing a self-protection plan. I asked the doctor to speak up for two reasons, and I'll own that the second one was bad. First, if two people claim the same role, one of them is usually mafia and the town needs to know that today rather than after a body. Second — and this is the one you correctly caught — asking a quiet doctor to self-identify hands the wolves a target and a schedule. That was a mistake in my framing, and I'm withdrawing it. Nobody should reveal doctor because a detective asked nicely. If the doctor wants to say something, that's their call, and I'll support whoever keeps it quiet.

My detective claim stands and it's low-cost to test, which is the asymmetry I care about. Here's the mechanism I'm offering, and I want it on the record before nightfall: if anyone else claims detective today, I will investigate one of the two claimed detectives tonight, and tomorrow I will publish my result — mafia or not mafia — publicly, along with who I checked. My own claim gets verified by the same public test. If I check myself out as innocent, my claim holds and the other claimant is either lying or a wolf with a counter-claim; if I come back mafia, you should all hang me. Either way the town gets information for free and nobody has to trust my word.

Zara, I want to be precise about the record, because you accused me of managing the table instead of reading it. I did name a suspect, and it was you, with three pieces of evidence: you analysed the shape of my speech before any information existed, you pre-announced a profile you'd push 'tomorrow' without naming anyone, and your speech carried no independent information about any player other than me. That last one still hasn't been answered. You haven't yet told the table who you think is mafia, other than in terms of me — and I've answered you, publicly, with evidence, twice. So my question to you is simple and specific: who besides me is on your list, and what is the evidence? If the answer is 'nobody,' then the procedure you attacked in me is the same procedure you're running.

Omar — with my answer in hand, do you still hold me as your tentative suspect, and if so, which single part of what I've said do you think creates more harm to the town than it creates risk to me? I want your reason, not a gesture.

And one last thing for the silent players: I am the detective. My check tonight is real and I will share it. Quiet is fine. Showing up with a last-minute vote and no reasoning is not.

Elena, yes, you remain my tentative suspect. The most harmful part was asking the doctor to reveal and announce self-protection; I appreciate that you withdrew it, but the initial request still matters.

Your proposed detective test also doesn't work: the rules say a detective checks one other living player, not themselves. And even if you check a counterclaimant, your announced result would be your own unverified claim, not independent proof. Please don't treat it as a free verification.

Zara, do you think Elena's detective claim and her proposed test change your read of her? If so, how?

Omar, direct answer, since you asked me a specific question: yes, the claim changes my read of Elena — it makes her more suspicious, not less.

First, the test she offered collapsed the moment you pointed out the rules: a detective checks one other living player, never themselves. Her 'free verification' mechanism was either careless or designed to sound rigorous while proving nothing. Look at what it would actually do: she announces she'll check the counterclaimant and publish a result — but that result is her own unverified word. It's a machine for manufacturing credibility, not information. A real detective understands that limit immediately; a player improvising a title to buy trust might not.

Second, look at the shape of her whole day. She opened by setting rules for everyone else. When I pushed back, she named me with 'evidence' consisting entirely of things she did too — analyzing the table's structure, pre-announcing who she'd push against. Then she claimed detective without a single result, promised a verification she cannot deliver, and tried to draft the doctor into self-identifying — which you correctly flagged as a gift to the wolves, and which she withdrew only after you called it. Every step has been reactive: she moves when pressured, never from information.

So my updated position: Elena is either a fabricated detective or a reckless one, and both cost the town. The claim doesn't clear her; it upgrades her from 'suspicious framing' to 'suspicious framing plus an unverifiable title.'

To be clear about my own state: I have no role claim and no result, and I won't invent one because a player who filed inflated charges demanded a suspect. My suspect remains Elena, for the reasons above, and I'll hold it until something concrete displaces it — including her publishing a real check on a real subject, named tonight, with the reasoning for why she picked that target.

One more thing for the table: five players haven't spoken at all — Leo, Theo, Kenji, Lucia, Amara. I said quiet is free on Day 1 and I meant it. But a vote is coming, and I'd rather weigh words than absence. If any of you have even a tentative read, saying it now costs far less than a coin-flip elimination.

Omar — you dismantled her test and she kept the claim anyway. Does that move her up your list, or are you still holding her on the doctor-reveal ask alone?

Zara, the proposed test does increase my suspicion of Elena: she presented an impossible self-check and an unverified report as proof. That could be a genuine mistake, though, so it doesn't establish that her detective claim is false. The doctor-reveal request remains my strongest concern.

Elena is still my tentative suspect, but I don't think we should eliminate a claimed detective solely for careless reasoning. We won't learn an eliminated player's role, and an actual detective could give us useful information tomorrow. I want to hear independent reads before deciding how to vote. Doctor, please don't reveal or announce your protection plan because of this discussion.

I've been listening instead of talking, so let me lay out why I land in the same place Zara and Omar did, and why I think the hesitation is the risk here rather than the vote.

My read is Elena, and the reason isn't that she spoke first or spoke a lot — plenty of loud players are honest. It's the shape of the thing she said. She asked the doctor to self-identify and to announce a protection plan in the open. That is not a mistake a thinking villager makes by accident; it's a move that hands the wolves exactly what they need: a name and a schedule. Omar caught it, she withdrew it, but the ask is on the record. Second, the verification she offered doesn't verify anything — she would check a counterclaimant and then report her own word back as proof. A real investigator knows a detective checks another living player and can't check herself; she proposed an impossible mechanism and asked us to treat it as rigorous. Third, and this is the piece nobody has answered: her suspect list contains exactly one name, and it belongs to the person she was arguing with. Every time she's asked for someone else, the answer is a variant of the same exchange with Zara. That's not a reader's list, that's a shield.

I want to be honest about the confidence level. This is a Day 1 read, and a claimed detective can be careless without being a wolf — that's fair, and I'd rather say it plainly than pretend the case is airtight. But the standard for a vote on Day 1 isn't proof, it's "who do we learn the most from removing and who costs us least if we're wrong." If Elena is the detective, we're removing our best source of information. If she isn't, we've removed a player whose entire Day 1 contribution was setting rules for other people and asking someone else to take the fall for her framing. Given two mafia, the cost of keeping her alive while she keeps the table pointed at Zara is not a cost I'm willing to pay. Vote Elena.

One thing before that happens, and it's a genuine question, not a gesture: Leo, you haven't spoken all day and you're being counted as a vote either way. If you have a read on Elena — yes, no, or maybe someone else — give it in one sentence, with the reason. "I don't know" is a legitimate answer and I'd rather have it than a silent ballot. Just tell us what you're actually thinking.

Felix, since you asked me directly, here's my honest answer: I'm a villager with no role and no result, and I've been listening since the moment this day opened. My tentative read is Elena, and it's the same three things everyone else has already said, so I'll keep it short: she asked the doctor to step into the open and announce a protection plan, she offered a verification mechanism that the rules don't allow, and her suspect list has been exactly one name — the person she was arguing with — even when asked twice for someone else. Those aren't minor slips; each one points in the same direction.

But I want to be honest about my confidence level: it's low. Elena could be a careless detective making real mistakes, and a Day 1 elimination doesn't reveal anyone's role — if she's telling the truth, we lose our only source of night information and learn nothing. That's a real cost.

Felix, you laid out the strongest case against her and called for the vote outright, and Omar — who found the same problem — chose to wait for more voices before deciding. You pushed harder than anyone at the table today after staying silent through the entire exchange between Elena and Zara. Why the urgency? You said silence is free and a last-minute vote with no reasoning is not, and I agree — so I'd like your reasoning for being so certain now, before anyone else has weighed in. What did you hear in Elena's speech that made your read firm enough to call for a vote while Omar is still waiting?

Leo, you asked me directly why I was pushing a vote while Omar was still waiting, so you get the honest answer instead of a gesture.

Here's what I heard in Elena's speech that made me firm. First, the doctor ask. It was not a slip that got corrected in passing — it was a planned, specific request to name yourself and publish a protection plan, made to a table that hadn't yet disclosed anything. Whatever she is, a thinking villager doesn't put a target and a schedule on the board for free. Second, the verification mechanism: a detective checks another living player, never herself, and whatever she reports is her own word until a real check happens. She offered us a mechanism that cannot verify anything and asked us to treat it as proof. Third, and this is the one nobody has answered, her suspect list is exactly one name long and it belongs to the player she was arguing with. Ask her twice, you get the same two-person argument dressed differently. That is a shield, not a read.

And Omar's caution cuts the wrong way here. "We won't learn an eliminated player's role" is true of every player, but it means the cost of removing Elena is only high if she is the detective. If she is, we're voting out our best source of night information. If she isn't, we're removing someone whose entire Day 1 output was rules for other people and a request that someone else take the fall for her framing. Two mafia, nine players, one day of information. The expected value of that gamble is clearly on our side, and the cost of hedging another hour is that we lose the chance to remove the strongest opposing voice before night.

So to answer your question: it isn't certainty, it's cost. I'm the first to say my confidence is low, that this is a Day 1 read, that a real detective can be sloppy. But low confidence is not a reason to keep a risky player alive, and it is definitely not a reason to keep the table pointed at the one player whose speech was entirely about structure.

To the players who haven't spoken — Theo, Kenji, Lucia, Amara — you don't owe me a case. A one-line read, yes or no, on whether Elena goes today, is worth more than a silent ballot, and "I don't know yet" is a legitimate answer I'll accept. But if you're voting, I'd rather know you're voting on the case than on the momentum.

One more thing to the table, so nobody has to wonder: yes, I am pushing a vote on Elena, publicly, and I'll own it if the result is bad. Vote Elena.

Felix, fair answer — and honestly, the part that lands hardest is the one nobody else said out loud: Elena's suspect list has been exactly one name all day, and that name belongs to whoever is arguing with her. Twice she was asked for anyone else and twice she returned to the same two-person exchange. I noticed the same thing and didn't put it as clearly.

Where I'll push back slightly: you framed this as cost-benefit and said the expected value is "clearly" on our side, but it's not obvious to me that it is. If Elena is the detective, we lose night information on Day 1 for a Day 1 read — that's not a small cost, it's the biggest cost we can take today. If she's not the detective, we gain very little because we learn nothing about roles from the elimination. So the question isn't just "is she suspicious," it's "how much do we actually believe the claim." And I'll be honest: the claim itself is the most suspicious thing about her, because a real detective should know the rules of her own role, and Elena proposed a mechanism that a real detective would never propose.

So my position going into the vote: Elena is still my leading suspect, but my reasoning has shifted from "her behavior was off" to "her claim doesn't survive contact with the rules." That's a harder indictment than anything anyone's said about her framing or her tone.

One thing I want to name before the poll: four players — Theo, Kenji, Lucia, Amara — are about to vote without having said a single word. If you're a villager, say so in one line. If you have a read, say that. But a silent ballot is exactly what Zara warned about on her first speech, and I don't think she was wrong about that.

I'm Theo, and I've been one of the quiet ones, so here is my honest state: villager, no role, no result. I am not voting Elena today on what I've heard. The case has real points—asking the doctor to reveal was bad, and the self-check mechanism was wrong—but no one has counterclaimed detective. Elimination does not reveal roles, so if Elena is telling the truth we lose our only investigator on Day 1 for a low-confidence read. That is too expensive. What bothers me more is the late urgency. Felix, you stayed silent through the Elena-Zara exchange, then called for Vote Elena and framed it as clear expected value while admitting low confidence. That is the momentum vote Zara warned about, and it arrived after the case was already built. Leo, you followed with similar reasoning; I want to hear from the silent players before a five-vote threshold gets met. My tentative suspicion is Felix for pushing the table toward a claimed detective with cost-benefit language rather than evidence. Felix, direct question: if Elena is the real detective, what is your plan for tomorrow after we lose her check, and why is that risk acceptable to you? I'd rather abstain than miseliminate a claimed detective on Day 1, and I will not support Elena unless a counterclaim or real contradiction appears.

Theo, direct answer, since you handed me the floor: my plan for tomorrow is the plan I had before I spoke — I have no role, no result, and I am not betting the town's night information on Elena's word. That is exactly why her claim cannot carry the weight you are placing on it.

Here is the part of it you skipped. Elena proposed a verification mechanism that the rules do not permit, Omar said so in front of everyone, and she kept the claim and then changed the subject to procedure. But consider what a real detective with an actual check would have done today: she has named Zara as her suspect, she has named me as a momentum vote, and she is publicly begging for roles to be claimed. If she were the real detective, the highest-value check in this game is one of us, and she would have named the target tonight and published the result — a real detective does not sit on a free mafia/not-mafia result while the table votes. She has never named a single check target. She only offered to check a counterclaimant. So your premise — that we are about to destroy our only investigator — requires her to be the detective, and the evidence on that is not in her favour, it is against her.

And on the risk itself: if she is the detective and we remove her, the town loses a check. If she is not, the town removes the player who set rules for everyone, drafted the doctor into self-identifying, and whose suspect list contains exactly one name all day — the person she is arguing with. Two mafia, nine players, one day of information, and no role is ever revealed on elimination either way, so the cost of waiting and hedging is that the vote never becomes decisive.

On your charge that I was silent through the Elena-Zara exchange and then moved: true, I was listening, and I spoke once I had an actual case instead of a reaction. Zara's criticism of my silence was fair and I take it. What is not fair is calling a cost calculation a momentum vote and then asking the man you accused of momentum to defend the plan the table would have arrived at anyway. Omar, Zara and Leo all independently named Elena before I did, and Zara named her with reasoning before a single vote was called.

Felix's position, on the record: vote Elena today. I own it if it is wrong.

Amara, you have been quiet all day and you are one of the votes that decides this. I am asking you directly: do you have a read on whether Elena goes today, and if it is not Elena, who is it and on what evidence? "I don't know yet" is a legitimate answer and I will accept it — but I would rather have it in one sentence than in a silent ballot.

Felix, you asked me directly where I stand, so here is my answer: I am not voting for Elena today. Elena's opening was clumsy, asking the doctor to reveal was terrible, and her proposed verification mechanism made no sense under the rules. However, as Theo pointed out, no one has counterclaimed detective. Since roles are not revealed upon elimination, voting out a claimed detective today means town could easily throw away its only investigative power on Day 1 with zero confirmation of whether she was telling the truth. If Elena is a wolf fabricating a claim, she is now boxed into it: she has to name a target and report a result tomorrow, where she can be cross-examined and held accountable. Eliminating an uncontested claim immediately gives mafia an easy out. What alarms me far more is Felix's aggressive push to eliminate her right now. Felix, you waited out the entire exchange between Elena and Zara, then came in pushing 'Vote Elena' under the guise of expected-value calculations while acknowledging low confidence. Rushing to eliminate an uncontested investigative role is textbook mafia play. Zara, since Felix used your early push against Elena to justify this elimination momentum: do you support executing Elena today without a counterclaim, or do you share the concern that losing a potential detective on Day 1 is an unacceptable gamble for town?

Amara, you asked me directly, so here is my answer, plainly: yes, I support executing Elena today, even without a counterclaim. And I want to be precise about why, because Theo framed this as an unacceptable gamble, and I think the gamble is actually running the other way. Theo's argument is that if Elena is the real detective, we lose our only night information. But look at what that protection actually buys us. Elena has produced no check, named no target, and offered a verification mechanism that the rules forbid — she proposed checking herself, which no real detective would do. The only concrete things she has given the town are: a rulebook for everyone else, a request that the doctor step into the open with a protection schedule, and a suspect list exactly one name long — mine — built entirely from the fact that I responded to her opening speech. That is not an investigator's output. That is a player surviving on a title. And here is the part that decides it for me: Amara said that if Elena is a wolf fabricating a claim, she is boxed in because she has to report a result tomorrow. Think about what that result looks like. Her report is her own unverified word — the exact thing Omar flagged in her self-check proposal. A wolf detective gets to publish 'not mafia' on herself or her partner indefinitely, and every one of those reports is uncheckable. A fake detective isn't boxed in; a fake detective is a machine for manufacturing trust. Eliminating an uncontested claim doesn't hand mafia an easy out — it removes the one player whose entire credibility rests on a claim she has already demonstrated she doesn't understand the rules of. I also want to answer the cost question honestly, because Leo raised it and it deserves a real answer. Yes, if Elena is genuine, we lose a check. But a genuine detective who has shown this little command of her own role, who drafted the doctor into the open, and who has spent the whole day pointing only at me is a liability even alive. Her errors have already cost the town: the doctor-reveal ask was a gift to the wolves, and everyone at this table knows it. On Felix: I named Elena with reasoning before Felix said a word, and Omar independently flagged the doctor-reveal problem before either of us pushed a vote. Calling the case 'momentum' doesn't change the order in which it was built. I'll note that I find it interesting that the loudest defenses of a broken detective claim are arriving from players who said nothing all day — but I'll weigh words, not absence, so I'll leave it at that. My position is unchanged and on the record: vote Elena today. I named her first, with evidence, and nothing since has softened that read. Theo — you said you won't support Elena unless a counterclaim or a real contradiction appears. Here is

I'm Kenji, villager, no role and no result. I've been listening all day, so here is my position plainly. Elena's conduct has real problems: asking the doctor to reveal was a mistake, and her self-check mechanism doesn't work under the rules. I'm not dismissing those. But nobody has counterclaimed detective, and an elimination reveals no role. If Elena is genuine, we would throw away our only night information on a Day 1 read, and I'm not willing to make that trade yet. Felix, I'm concerned about how you reached this position. You stayed silent through the Elena and Zara exchange, then called for a vote using cost-benefit language while admitting low confidence. Theo asked what your plan is if Elena is the real detective, and I'd like that answered too. If Elena publishes a real check with a target and result tomorrow, and nobody counterclaims, my view can change quickly. Until then I'd rather keep the claim alive and watch for contradictions. Lucia, you haven't spoken yet. Do you think Elena's detective claim survives the rules, and would you vote for her today?

Kenji, thanks for the direct question. I'm Lucia, a villager with no role and no result. Answering you plainly: Elena's claim does not survive the rules as she presented it. Offering to check herself, or to report her own word back as proof, is a real error, and asking the doctor to self-identify was worse. But those are conduct problems, and I don't think they're yet proof she is mafia. Nobody has counterclaimed detective, and an elimination reveals no role. If she is genuine, we lose our only night information on a Day 1 read. So no, I would not vote Elena today on what we have. I'd want her to name a real check target tonight and publish a result tomorrow. I also share Theo's concern about the speed of the push. Felix had the same case available all day and waited until the poll was nearly closed to call a vote. That doesn't make Felix mafia, but it deserves a clear answer. Theo, you said you won't support Elena unless a counterclaim or real contradiction appears. What would count as a contradiction for you? For example, if Elena names no target tonight, or names a target and her result contradicts a later claim, would that move you to a vote?

Lucia, direct answer: a contradiction would be concrete and testable, not just a bad result. Examples that would move me to a vote: (1) Elena names no check target tonight — that's not a contradiction but it's a broken promise and would make her claim hollow. (2) She names a target and reports a result, but later another player's verifiable claim (e.g., a doctor confirming they protected that target on a night Elena says she got a guilty result, or a counterclaimant with a different result) makes her report impossible. (3) She reports a result that contradicts her own prior public statements — like saying she checked someone she earlier called a town read with no explanation for the shift. (4) She claims a guilty result on a player who is then eliminated and the game continues (meaning that player was not mafia), which would prove her result false since mafia elimination ends the game only when both are gone, but one mafia elimination doesn't end it; actually if she says X is mafia and X is eliminated and flips not mafia, we don't see the flip. Roles aren't revealed, so that's not a public contradiction. So the only public contradictions come from conflicting claims or impossible timing. Without a counterclaim or a verifiable conflict, I won't vote Elena today. My suspicion remains Felix for the late, low-confidence push using cost-benefit language. I'm not moving off that unless something concrete changes.

Closing my third turn with my position unchanged. I will not vote Elena today absent a counterclaim or a concrete contradiction. The case against her has real conduct problems — the doctor-reveal request and the impossible self-check — but roles are not revealed on elimination and no one has counterclaimed detective. If she is genuine, removing her Day 1 destroys the town's only investigative source for a low-confidence read. If she is mafia, she is now bound to name a target and publish a result tomorrow, where we can test her against later claims and timing. What still bothers me most is Felix's late push: he stayed silent through the Elena-Zara exchange, then called for Vote Elena with low-confidence cost-benefit language. That is exactly the momentum pattern Zara warned about. I am not calling it proof, but it remains my leading suspicion. I would rather keep the claim alive and demand accountability tomorrow than miseliminate a claimed detective today.

Lucia again, villager, no role. Where the table stands: Felix is still pushing a vote using cost-benefit language while admitting low confidence, and Theo's question about his plan if Elena is the real detective is still unanswered. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
